prediction:
The report by William L. Painter, titled "Congress at times has sought to ascertain how much the government spends on securing the homeland," examines the history of efforts by Congress to understand the budget for homeland security initiatives. The report highlights the complexity of the issue, as homeland security spending is spread across multiple agencies and programs. Painter notes that the 9/11 attacks led to a significant increase in homeland security funding, but that the lack of a clear definition of what constitutes homeland security spending has made it difficult for Congress to accurately track and allocate resources.

The report also discusses the role of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in managing homeland security initiatives and the ongoing debate over the extent of DHS management involvement in the functioning of departmental components. Painter notes that some policy experts have advocated for a strong management function at DHS, while others have supported a more limited role that allows DHS components to function independently.

Despite the challenges, Painter notes that there have been efforts to improve coordination and unity of effort within DHS. For example, former Secretary Jeh Johnson issued a memorandum in 2014 that called for reforms to strengthen departmental unity of effort and promote greater efficiency and effectiveness across the department. These reforms included the establishment of a Unity of Effort Award and the provision of statutory authority to DHS for certain activities connected with the Unity of Effort initiative.

Looking ahead, Painter notes that Congress may continue to debate the appropriate role of departmental management at DHS and the progress of management reforms. He suggests that Congress may wish to follow up on the Secretary's priorities as outlined in her pre-confirmation questionnaire and assess the effectiveness of current unity of effort programs and processes. Overall, the report underscores the importance of effective management and coordination in ensuring that the government is able to effectively address the complex and evolving threats to homeland security.

answers: In 2001, in the wake of the terrorist attacks of September 11, "homeland security" went from being a concept discussed among a relatively small cadre of policymakers and strategic thinkers to one broadly discussed among policymakers, including a broad swath of those in Congress. Debates over how to implement coordinated homeland security policy led to the passage of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (P.L. 107-296), the establishment of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), and extensive legislative activity in the ensuing years. Initially, homeland security was largely seen as counterterrorism activities. Today, homeland security is a broad and complex network of interrelated issues, in policymaking terms. For example, in its executive summary, the Quadrennial Homeland Security Review issued in 2014 delineated the missions of the homeland security enterprise as follows: prevent terrorism and enhance security; secure and manage the borders; enforce and administer immigration laws; safeguard and secure cyberspace; and strengthen national preparedness and resilience. This report compiles a series of Insights by CRS experts across an array of homeland security issues that may come before the 116th Congress. Several homeland security topics are also covered in CRS Report R45500, Transportation Security: Issues for the 116th Congress. The information contained in the Insights only scratches the surface of these selected issues. Congressional clients may obtain more detailed information on these topic and others by contacting the relevant CRS expert listed in CRS Report R45684, Selected Homeland Security Issues in the 116th Congress: CRS Experts.
